sentences: In a tall, narrow picture, Kannon, the Buddhist figure of compassion, floats in the air, and below, at her feet, there is a newborn infant.
Kannon is looking down at the child.
This is Hibo Kannon, painted in 1888 by the Japanese artist Kanō Hōgai.
Hōgai was born in 1828 in what is now Yamaguchi Prefecture and trained as a painter of the Kanō school.
After the Meiji Restoration, commissions dried up, and he made a living with jobs such as drawing designs for export ceramics.
His fortunes changed in 1882, when the American scholar Ernest Fenollosa noticed his work.
In 1886 he travelled with Okakura Tenshin to study old temples in Nara, and the sketches of Kannon statues he made there are said to lie behind the face in this painting.
Start with Kannon at the top.
She hangs in the air, bending her gaze downward.
The title calls her a merciful mother, but that name is said to have been given later, not by Hōgai himself.
Look at her hands.
In one she holds a willow branch, and in the other a crystal vase.
A Kannon holding a willow branch is known as a Willow Kannon.
Clear water falls from the vase.
The infant receiving these drops is not found in earlier pictures of Kannon, so it is usually seen as Hōgai's own invention.
Now look lower, at the infant by Kannon's feet.
The child is often read as a new life about to descend into the human world.
Mountains appear in the picture too, so a believable space and a floating, unreal world overlap.
The materials are traditional mineral pigments on silk.
He used no Western pigments, and drew even the outlines in colour rather than ink.
Layer upon layer of colour gives a soft tone close to a pastel drawing, and gold dust is scattered across the surface.
Yet the picture also has depth and volume.
Fenollosa had encouraged Hōgai to learn Western perspective and ways of showing space, and this work is seen as an attempt to bring light and shadow into a traditional style.
Hōgai had been chosen to teach at the new Tokyo School of Fine Arts, but on 5 November 1888 he died before it opened.
Accounts say this was four days after he finished the painting, and that his friend Hashimoto Gahō added the last gold dust.
That is why it carries no signature.
It was his last painting, and it is often called the starting point of modern Japanese painting.
It was named an Important Cultural Property in 1955 and now belongs to the University Art Museum of Tokyo University of the Arts.
Step back and take in Kannon above and the infant below in a single view.
Remembering that a painter near the end of his life chose to paint a new life, how does the picture look to you now?
